newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian insurance regulators must welcome new players - minister.
newsitem.headline: Asian insurance regulators must welcome new players - minister.

text.p: Asia's insurance regulators may be wary of new players in their markets but must welcome liberalisation in order to foster competition, Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu told industry leaders on Tuesday.
"Regulators fear the potential destabilising effects of the introduction of new players to their markets," Hu said as he opened the 18th East Asian Insurance Congress in Singapore.

But it was vital that regulators face the challenge of liberalisation or "risk fostering an uncompetitive insurance industry unable to meet the growing, and increasingly sophisticated, insurance needs of the region's dynamic economies," he said.
The insurance industry in Asia has grown rapidly in tandem with economic expansion in the region.

In Singapore alone, the industry has posted double-digit growth over the last five years. Though growth has slowed, in 1995 total insurance premiums rose to Singapore $6.4 billion (US$4.5 billion) from S$5.7 billion in 1994.

The massive potential has attracted many well-capitalised foreign insurance companies, but Hu warned that while they bring much-needed capacity and skill to the region, the tougher competition could lead to the collapse of local companies.
"The increased competition may particularly affect indigenous companies who tend to be small with insufficient resources and skills to match the clout of insurers from developed markets," said Hu.
"This creates the possibility of these weaker insurers failing, and in the process causing considerable disruption to the market and the economy as a whole."

He said the Singapore government had consciously avoided interfering in the conduct of insurance business, but emphasised his belief in the importance of a strong regulatory framework in a competitive market.
"Without a proper regulatory framework, such a market environment may lead to chaotic conditions with potentially devastating consequences for policyholders," he said.
